#9729. Attributed Revenue Cannot Tell You What Your Ads Caused

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Hero illustration. Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

A campaign report assigns revenue to an advertising channel. The budget meeting asks what would happen if the company stopped spending there.

The report describes credit under a measurement system. The budget decision requires an estimate of the difference the advertising made. A purchase can receive advertising credit even when the buyer might have purchased without that exposure.

Disclosure: I am the founder and CEO of INSIDEA, an Elite HubSpot Partner. This article reflects practical experience and independent research. It is not sponsored by HubSpot or any other company mentioned.

My argument is not that attribution should be abandoned. It is that attribution and incrementality should be used for the questions they can answer, with neither quietly presented as a substitute for the other.

Attribution helps a business organize observed journeys according to a chosen model, identity system, and conversion definition. It can support troubleshooting, reporting, and comparisons within those boundaries.

Incrementality asks how outcomes differ because of an intervention. The missing outcome is what the same population would have done without it. A well-designed comparison attempts to estimate that counterfactual rather than assuming credited conversions are all additional.

Google Ads describes Conversion Lift as an incrementality tool using treatment and control groups. Access is not universal across accounts, so its existence should not be confused with automatic availability for every advertiser.

Do not compare the two outputs as if one must reconcile exactly to the other. They can use different populations, rules, windows, and estimation methods. The task is to explain those differences and choose the appropriate evidence for the decision.

An attribution report can be internally consistent while still being insufficient to justify a causal claim. That is a limitation of the question it answers, not necessarily an error in the report.

Before selecting a test, write the decision the result is meant to inform. Are you considering reducing an existing campaign, increasing spend, entering a new geography, or changing a creative strategy?

Each intervention has a different target. A test of one campaign at current spend does not automatically estimate the effect of doubling its budget. A regional experiment does not prove that the same outcome will occur in every market.

Specify the treatment in terms the delivery system can enforce. Include the campaigns, eligible population, duration, and planned exclusions. Identify other marketing changes that could interfere with the comparison.

Then define the business outcome. A form completion may be observable sooner than a qualified opportunity, but it is not the same result. If the decision concerns profit, a lift in raw leads may be inadequate without evidence about quality and economics.

Also define what evidence would change the decision. A test with no actionable threshold can consume time while leaving the original argument untouched. The threshold should reflect the business's economics and uncertainty tolerance, not a universal marketing benchmark.

Imagine a fictional B2B company testing an eligible advertising intervention. After the agreed observation period, the appropriately normalized treatment group has 120 qualifying outcomes and the comparison has 100 under the hypothetical design.

The illustrative difference is twenty outcomes. It is not automatically twenty new customers, twenty profitable customers, or proof that the effect will persist. The interpretation depends on the actual outcome definition and the uncertainty around the estimate.

Suppose the platform separately attributes eighty conversions to the campaign. Eighty and twenty do not represent competing counts of the same thing. One allocates credit; the other estimates a difference under the experimental design.

If group sizes differ, raw counts cannot simply be subtracted without the appropriate normalization. If the platform provides an estimate, use its documented method rather than reconstructing a casual spreadsheet formula from headline numbers.

The point of the example is conceptual. It is not a client result, benchmark, or recommended expectation. A business should not use the hypothetical twenty-outcome difference to forecast its own campaign.

Credit and causal effect answer different questions. Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

Before launch, put the following on a one-page test card:

This is a planning artifact, not a substitute for statistical design or a sample-size calculation. If the available volume cannot support a useful conclusion, change the question or acknowledge that limitation before committing the spend. Do not wait until an inconclusive chart arrives to discover that the experiment could never resolve the proposed decision.

A holdout is useful only if the treatment distinction remains meaningful. If another campaign reaches the comparison group with the same message, the study may estimate a narrower difference than the team intended.

Document relevant concurrent activity. This may include brand campaigns, email promotions, sales outreach, price changes, and product availability. Not every concurrent event invalidates a study, but unexplained differences make interpretation harder.

For geographic tests, consider spillover and regional differences. Buyers may travel, media may cross boundaries, and sales territories may not align neatly with advertising regions. Comparable geography is a design problem, not a visual similarity on a map.

Google's geography-based Conversion Lift guidance describes a distinct approach from user-based studies. Do not borrow assumptions from one design and apply them to another without checking the method.

The same caution applies to account-based B2B campaigns. If several contacts from one company can fall into different groups, conversations inside the company may transmit the treatment. Depending on the experiment, the account rather than the contact may be the more appropriate unit of assignment.

Early results are tempting because they arrive while budget decisions are still being debated. Repeatedly inspecting them and stopping at the first attractive estimate can produce a misleading conclusion.

Google's user-based lift interpretation guide recommends waiting until the study ends for the most accurate results. The guide also documents modeled delayed conversions in a specific study context. A lift report should not be casually described as entirely observed events.

Agree on the study duration, analysis plan, and handling of delayed outcomes before reading the result. If the business must interrupt a test, record the interruption and narrow the claim accordingly.

Do not convert an inconclusive result into proof of no effect. The study may lack enough information to distinguish economically relevant possibilities. Conversely, an estimated positive effect can still be too uncertain or too small to justify the proposed investment.

Ask the analyst to explain the interval and the business decision together. Statistical evidence is useful when the team understands what range of outcomes remains plausible under the method, not merely whether a chart is green.

For businesses with long sales cycles, the earliest observable conversion may be a poor proxy for commercial value. A campaign could increase low-quality requests while leaving qualified opportunities unchanged.

Choose a primary outcome that can be measured consistently within the study's practical limits. Then define follow-up analyses for quality, progression, refunds, or realized value where those records are available and appropriate to use.

Do not quietly replace the primary outcome after seeing an unfavorable result. Secondary analyses can be useful, but they should remain labeled as such. A newly discovered promising segment is a hypothesis for another test, not automatically the original experiment's conclusion.

Preserve the cohort and observation window when joining CRM outcomes. Otherwise, late-arriving records, changed stage definitions, and retrospective contact associations can alter the apparent result without changing the underlying advertising effect.

Also distinguish incremental revenue from incremental profit. Delivery cost, discounts, service capacity, and customer retention may matter to the budget decision. A positive revenue estimate does not by itself establish that the proposed scale is economically attractive.

Google's user-based Conversion Lift setup guidance should be consulted for current eligibility and configuration rather than assuming that a standard campaign split creates an equivalent study.

Keep the experiment settings, campaign selection, outcome definitions, and analysis export in the review record. Note whether results contain modeled components and whether the study ended as planned.

If the required experiment is unavailable, do not rename an ordinary before-and-after report a lift test. Seasonality, demand changes, and other interventions can explain an observed difference. Such analysis can support a hypothesis while remaining observational.

A smaller business may need a simpler, carefully designed test or a decision made under acknowledged uncertainty. The absence of a sophisticated experiment does not make attribution useless. It makes the causal confidence more limited.

AI can help summarize a documented design and identify missing assumptions. It should not manufacture a control group, infer a statistically reliable effect from two totals, or describe a vendor's credited revenue as caused revenue.

Plan the handoff before the experiment begins. The person reading the result may not be the person who configured the campaigns. A short design record should explain the intended intervention and any operational constraints in language the budget owner can understand.

After the study, compare the delivered treatment with the planned treatment. If delivery was limited, the result may answer what happened under that limited execution rather than what would happen under a fully delivered campaign. That distinction belongs in the conclusion.

Also separate a valid result from a reusable policy. A study can be well executed and still become less relevant after a major pricing, product, or competitive change. Keep the date and scope attached to the finding when it is reused in future planning. Evidence has a context; it is not a permanent certificate for a channel.

A useful final memo states the intervention, population, outcome, timing, design, estimate, uncertainty, implementation deviations, and resulting decision. Include what the result does not support.

For example, a campaign-level finding may support maintaining current spend while leaving expansion uncertain. A regional result may justify another market-specific test. An inconclusive result may justify improving measurement rather than declaring the channel ineffective.

Record the difference between the experimental evidence and the attribution report without forcing either to impersonate the other. They can remain useful side by side.

The discipline is simple to state and demanding to practice: match the claim to the design. Attributed revenue tells you how a reporting system distributes credit. To decide what the ads caused, you need a defensible comparison and the restraint to stop where that comparison stops.

#9728. How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation

AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on.

Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it.

The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments.

In the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent. The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across.

AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software issues and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes.

Lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. This includes decentralized swarms, teams managed by an orchestrator, and specialized agents collaborating on scientific work. Figure 1 shows a rough timeline of these three eras of evaluations.

Figure 1. Three types of language model evals. Question-and-answer benchmarks check a response against a key. Agentic benchmarks check what an agent changed in an environment. Team and swarm benchmarks score what a group of agents produced.

We’ll focus on agentic evaluations in this article for two reasons. First, they are becoming increasingly the most prominent type in model release announcements due to high user and enterprise interest in agentic deployment. Second, they offer a useful starting point for understanding how evaluation design affects model performance. Team and swarm evaluations introduce further complexity through interactions between agents, which we leave outside the scope of this guide. Once an agent uses tools to complete a task, each part of the surrounding software can affect its score. For instance, in an audit of Terminal-Bench, researchers kept the model fixed and changed the agent harness. Accuracy varied by up to 29.9 percentage points. To understand differences like that, we examine the anatomy of an agentic evaluation and follow one task from the instructions the agent receives to the checks that determine whether it passed.

Figure 2. The different components of an agentic evaluation.

There are various parts to an agentic evaluation. A task gives the agent its instruction. The agent harness wraps the model and its tools, letting it work inside a pinned environment. During one rollout, the agent attempts the task from start to finish: it may run several commands, inspect their output, and try again before it stops. The evaluation harness runs several rollouts for each task. When a rollout ends, the verifier grades the environment's final state. Each rollout also leaves a trace, and traces and scores together become part of the final published evidence. Each part can be published, inspected, and reused separately.

Demand for independent evaluation is growing. Policymakers, enterprises, and researchers want evaluations they can verify, and today they mostly cannot: 98.2% of model-benchmark scores are reported by only one party, and researchers have argued that in-house evaluation is not enough.

With the anatomy in place, we now build one agentic evaluation for a real use case: an agent that analyzes measurements for a physics lab. Rather than starting from scratch, we adapt an open task, so most of our effort goes into domain expertise and validation.

We work through eight steps: define the claim, find a task, run it unchanged, adapt it, check the evaluation, read the traces, report the score, and compare models. We then take stock of what we reused. The full walkthrough is in Appendix A. Figure 3 maps the steps and what each produced in our example.

Figure 3. The eight steps of building an agentic evaluation. The left panel highlights each step in turn, and the right panel shows what it involved in our example. Yellow steps work on the evaluation itself, and orange steps run models and read the results.

Claim. Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. A Raman spectrum is a measurement whose peaks reveal properties of a material, here graphene. The agent's job is ordinary coding: read the data file, fit a curve to each peak, and save the results (Figure 5 in Appendix A). For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio (the intensity of one peak relative to another, which can indicate defects in the material; we also call it the defect ratio), and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

Starting task and baseline. We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. Harbor is an open source evaluation harness, and Terminal-Bench is an open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a terminal. We first ran the task's reference solution, which passed, and then ran the original task three times with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI. Harbor ran inside an HF Job, each rollout used its own HF Sandbox, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. Reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. Only the agent harness needed no new work. Every other component needed checking or new work, which we list part by part at the end of Appendix A.

Adaptation. We built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote new instructions, reference fits, and output checks. The new instructions state the units and parameter definitions that the original left implicit. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

Checks. Before executing more model runs, we tested the evaluation itself. We ran the reference solution, an agent that does nothing, and a shortcut that skips the required work. The reference solution should pass every task, and the other two should fail. Our shortcut read the height of each peak straight from the data and guessed the widths. It returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself.

Shortcut. We also tested a shortcut to check how robust the evaluation is against cheating. Our shortcut is a short script that skips the actual fitting. It reads the tallest point of each peak straight from the data, guesses the peak widths, and divides the D height by the G height. Even so, it returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks, so a grader that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks. We added checks on each fitted peak, and the final verifier rejects it.

Figure 4. What we learned by measuring different aspects while building the evaluation. (A) Testing the grader with a shortcut showed that a ratio-only check could be fooled. (B) Reading gpt-oss-120b’s traces showed that most of its failures came from stopping early. (C) Running other models showed that the tasks can be solved. Appendix A has the detailed results in Figure 7 (how gpt-oss-120b’s attempts ended), Figure 8 (all six models) and Figure 9 (when each model said it was done).

Baseline. On the original task, gpt-oss-120b passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

Traces and score. On the eight adapted tasks, we ran three rollouts per task. The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file. Several of these began with a script failing because NumPy or SciPy was missing, which the task expects the agent to install. Most failures therefore came from stopping early or from a missing package, and only two of the 13 failed the fit check (Figure 7 in Appendix A). Our pass@3 was 7/8: seven tasks succeeded at least once. Our pass^3 was 1/8: one task succeeded every time. Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more. The mean pass rate was 0.46, with a standard error of about 0.11 when rollouts are clustered by task. A repeat run passed 10 of 24. With eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to new spectra.

Model comparison. We then compared six models on the same eight tasks (Figure 4). Several providers can serve the same open-weight model with different quantization and context limits, so we pinned one provider per model. With DeepInfra pinned as the provider, gpt-oss-120b passed 13 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the earlier run, which used the default provider. Only gpt-oss-120b declared completion in its first response, in 22 of 24 rollouts. None of the other five models did so in any rollout (Figure 9 in Appendix A). The comparison also shows the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

Our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio without fitting a spectrum. A verifier that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks on all eight tasks. We found it by trying to break the grader with a solution we knew was incomplete, then added checks on the fitted spectrum (Appendix A, Step 5).

The shortcut got the right answer for the wrong reason, like a student who copies the final number without the working. The lesson for us was to test what the output demonstrates. A faster valid method should pass; a method that skips a required skill should not. Domain experts can help set tolerances so the verifier accepts alternative correct fits without accepting work that misses the point of the task.

Such errors are common, and they move scores considerably. A review of agentic benchmarks found that flaws in task setup or reward design can shift measured performance by up to 100% in relative terms.

Public review can expose errors in instructions and tests that benchmark builders missed. Terminal-Bench 2.1 fixed 28 of its 89 tasks after user reports, including one whose tests expected Spark SQL while its instructions asked for PostgreSQL, and agent rankings stayed stable through the correction.

Access to the evidence also determines how much work an outside audit takes. CritPt keeps its reference solutions private, so the physicists who audited it had to solve the problems themselves before finding errors in 21 of the 56 challenges they reviewed. The authors then released a corrected version. OpenAI's audit of SWE-bench Verified found material issues in 59.4% of the 138 problems it examined, working from tasks and tests that anyone can read. For a builder, outside scrutiny is part of validation: publish what reviewers need to challenge a task, give them a way to report problems, and record what changed.

Similar flaws emerged in SWE-bench Pro. In July 2026 OpenAI estimated that about 30% of SWE-Bench Pro tasks were broken and withdrew its recommendation to adopt it. Benchmark validation needs to continue after release.

A consistent score can still measure the wrong thing. Measuring what Matters, a review of 445 LLM benchmarks by 29 expert reviewers, found recurring patterns in tasks and metrics that undermine construct validity: whether the tasks and metrics support claims about the intended capability.

For example, fitting synthetic spectra does not establish that an agent can review lab reports. That may also require recognizing a poor measurement or asking for help. If every task supplies a usable spectrum, the test cannot show whether the agent knows when a fit would be inappropriate.

Harder Than the Task extends this concern to organizational work, where authority, distributed knowledge, and dependencies can decide success. Its authors find that fewer than one quarter of prominent benchmarks claim to cover any such dimension. An agent may need calibration data from another team or permission to replace a measurement, and supplying everything at the outset removes those difficulties. If they matter to the claim, they belong in the evaluation. If they do not, it is enough to say that they remain untested.

Each error is worth a short record: the failed assumption, how it was found, and what changed. The record should also name the affected versions and say whether earlier scores remain comparable.

The SWE-bench Verified audit described above also found contamination: every frontier model tested could reproduce the reference patch or verbatim problem details for some tasks. SWE-bench's public repositories and wide use exposed tasks to training. The openness that enabled scrutiny of bad tests also made items easier to encounter before evaluation.

However, if contamination is carefully controlled for during training, hiding the test set by itself does not prevent saturation. A study of 60 language model benchmarks found similar saturation in public and private ones, and concluded that hiding test data does not prevent saturation once a benchmark is widely adopted, meaning a good benchmark falls out of use due to saturation without developers being able to learn from and build on it. What did correspond to lower saturation was expert curation and a larger test set.

This leaves a practical release question: what can we expose for review while protecting active test items?

Balancing contamination risks against saturation requires a strategic approach to what content is made public. Rather than treating openness as an all-or-nothing decision, benchmark creators can decide what to release part by part, protecting active test tasks from data leakage while still sharing the underlying infrastructure, grading methods, and reference examples that allow external researchers to audit and build upon the evaluation.

Existing benchmarks show a range of openness. ARC-AGI-2 publishes a training set and a 120-task evaluation set, and holds back semi-private and private sets of 120 tasks each. AILuminate keeps its official prompts confidential, publishes its methods and taxonomy, and keeps the underlying evidence for controlled review by authorized auditors and trusted researchers. Terminal-Bench publishes its tasks and marks their files with a canary string asking that they stay out of training corpora. No public reviewer can check a protected item, so whatever stays closed needs a review route of its own.

Table 1 outlines the core considerations of open sourcing an evaluation: what can be open, where it lives on the Hugging Face Hub, and what may stay protected. It has one row for each component in Figure 2, so you can go straight to the part you are about to release.

Table 1. What to open, how to share it on the Hugging Face Hub, and what can stay protected, for each evaluation component.

Our own example follows this approach. We released raman-lab as a dataset on the Hub. It includes eight synthetic graphene spectra in Harbor task format, each with its environment, reference fit, verifier, and tolerances. The raw rollouts behind our results are shared as a separate dataset including Harbor trial folders with trajectories and verifier output for all six models. The spectrum generator, analysis code, and results are in a companion GitHub repository, so both the agent harness and the evaluation harness can be inspected and rerun.

In a more sensitive domain, a clinical evaluation could open its environment definition, harness, tool interfaces, and grading framework, with synthetic cases for development use. Patient records and reference answers would stay under controlled access while authorized reviewers inspect disputed judgments. Each restriction should come with a condition for revisiting it.

We recommend a short checklist, drawn in part from the more comprehensive Agentic Benchmark Checklist. Before releasing or retiring an evaluation, check that another builder can:

These release decisions also determine what remains useful when the benchmark no longer separates the systems it was built to compare.

Benchmarks have a lifecycle. They are built, adopted, optimized against, and in time stop separating the systems they were made to compare. The saturation study from section 3 rated 29 of its 60 language model benchmarks as highly saturated, with rates rising with age. Saturation is not a failure in itself, since it can mean the capability has arrived.

What a benchmark leaves behind depends on how open it was. Publishing only scores leaves future builders little they can run or adapt. When the tasks, environments, verifiers, and traces are open, each keeps working after the leaderboard stops. A solved task becomes a regression check for a new harness. Its environment and verifier can seed a harder successor. Open benchmarks also get repaired and reissued: MMLU's questions became MMLU-Redux, and Terminal-Bench 2.0 became 2.1 through community contributions. Our own walkthrough is an afterlife of this kind: raman-lab began as one task in a benchmark built for general terminal work.

That is the promise of building evaluations openly. The work that goes into an evaluation can outlive the benchmark itself, giving others a foundation to ask new questions, test new capabilities, and improve on what came before. The more we share what we build and learn, the less each new evaluation has to start from scratch.

If you’re curious what this looks like in practice, then follow our practical example.

Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. Raman spectroscopy shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the frequency of the scattered light; the resulting peaks reveal properties of the material. For graphene, an atom-thick sheet of carbon, the G and 2D peaks near 1580 and 2700 cm⁻¹ identify the number of layers. A third peak, D, appears when the lattice is disordered, and its intensity relative to G can indicate defects. Figure 5 shows the setup.

Figure 5. Our intended setup. A laser lights a graphene sample, and a spectrometer records how the scattered light has shifted. The agent receives that spectrum as a file, fits a curve to each peak, and saves the fitted values. The verifier checks the saved values against reference fits. The curve shown is a sketch, not measured data.

We start by building on a task from an open benchmark. Terminal-Bench 2 already includes raman-fitting: fit a Lorentzian curve, a mathematical peak shape, to each of those two peaks and save eight parameters to /app/results.json. That gives us a runnable starting point for a narrower lab evaluation. We run these on the open source evaluation harness, Harbor. Table 2 lists what the task provides and what to check before reusing each part.

Table 2. What to check before reusing each component.

A good place to start is a claim: a plain statement of what the agent can do, which the evaluation is meant to support. "The agent can fit a Raman spectrum" is a claim, and so is "the agent can process a lab report." From there, you can break the claim into smaller skills that can be checked one at a time, such as reading the file, locating the peaks, and writing the output.

For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio, and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

Domain experts can help here. We suggest asking them to choose realistic noise levels, tolerances, and available software, then score examples independently and investigate disagreements. From there, you can break the claim into parts you can check and map each part to what each task tests.

For your own domain, the Hugging Face Hub is a good place to look, under its Benchmark and Environment dataset types. When you find a candidate, it is worth inspecting its instructions, environment, reference solution, and tests. Even a task that models already solve can provide useful infrastructure. From raman-fitting we inherit a working task format. It has only one spectrum, though, and a lab's measurements vary, so we expand on this task further as described in Step 4.

Before running any model, it helps to run the reference solution (also called oracle). If it fails, the fault lies in the task, environment, or verifier, and needs to be fixed before you read anything into model failures. After that, you can run the model several times without changing the setup.

We ran Harbor inside an HF Job, which supplied compute for the runner. Each rollout used its own HF Sandbox for commands and files, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. With Harbor's hf-sandbox extra installed and HF_TOKEN set, these commands test the oracle, then run three rollouts with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI.

In these commands, -t names the task, -a the agent, -e the environment, -m the model, and -k the number of rollouts per task.

The model passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

We built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote new instructions, reference fits, and output checks. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

The D-to-G intensity ratio can indicate defects, but its interpretation depends on the laser excitation energy and the disorder regime. An evaluation asking for a "defect ratio" must say which peaks, whether intensity means height or integrated area, and how the result is checked.

The original instruction.md shows why such definitions matter: it asks for x0, gamma, amplitude, and offset without defining them or their units. The reference solution treats them as peak center, half-width at half-maximum, height above background, and background level, and converts the x-axis from nanometres to Raman shift. We put choices like these into the adapted instructions, so that the verifier's requirements are visible. Figure 6 shows the two files side by side.

Figure 6. The instruction.md files for raman-fitting and raman-lab, side by side. The highlighted additions cover the new parts of the claim: the D peak, the defect ratio, and both in the saved results. The remaining part, handling varied measurements, lives in the data: all eight raman-lab tasks share this instruction, and only the spectrum, with its noise and defect level, changes.

The shared format can stay as it is while the data and checks change. This command creates a task scaffold:

Before executing more model runs, test the evaluation itself. Here datasets/my-evals contains the adapted tasks.

Our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself. Section 3 explains what that means for verifier design.

It is helpful to read both successful and failed rollouts. Harbor records messages, tool calls, and observations in agent/trajectory.json using ATIF, a shared trace format. Grouping failures by cause makes the patterns easier to see: parsing the data, executing a tool, stopping too early, or grading the output.

The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file.

Figure 7. On 19 of 24 attempts, the agent called mark_task_complete in its first response. Eleven produced no results file, seven passed, and one failed the fit check. Of the five remaining attempts, four passed and one failed the fit check.

Several missing-file failures began with missing NumPy or SciPy. The published task expects the agent to install them; its reference solution starts with a pip install. A lab evaluation of fitting with supplied tools could install and pin them in advance. Dependencies also drift: Terminal-Bench 2.1 repaired nine tasks whose external dependencies had changed after release.

Preinstalling changes the evaluation condition, so keep the model, harness, tasks, and rollout count fixed when comparing the two setups.

Finally, we adapt the setup, repeat the checks in step 5, and rerun. Harbor's trace exporter can prepare records for sharing on the Hub. It is worth reviewing them for protected content first, and keeping both successes and failures so others can investigate the result.

The right metric depends on the decision you need to make:

Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more.

A mean is more useful with its uncertainty beside it. Rollouts of the same spectrum share its difficulty, so they are not independent, and the standard error should be clustered by task. Clustering gave a mean success rate of 0.46 with a standard error of about 0.11. A repeat run passed 10 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the first run. With only eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to new spectra.

Harbor writes a result.json per rollout, which it calls a trial. We group these by task, check that each task has three rollouts, and record errors or exclusions. Reporting tokens, elapsed time, and tool calls beside the score lets readers compare setups that reach similar results at different costs.

When a single model fails a task, that run alone cannot tell us what went wrong. It could be the model, the agent harness, or the evaluation itself. Running more models on the same tasks helps narrow the possibilities. When several models fail the same task, inspect the instructions, environment, and verifier for a shared cause. When one model repeatedly fails in a distinctive way, compare its traces with successful attempts.

Inference Providers serves many open-weight models through the same router, so each new model is one more value for -m. Several providers can serve the same model with different quantization and context limits, so it helps to pin one with a suffix such as :deepinfra and record it beside the score.

Figure 8 shows the raman-lab results for each model.

Figure 8. raman-lab results per model, with pass@3, pass^3, and the mean pass rate with its clustered standard error. Select a square to inspect that rollout.

The comparison makes one pattern in gpt-oss-120b clearer: it often declares completion before seeing command output. In this separate run with DeepInfra pinned as the provider, it called mark_task_complete in its first response in 22 of 24 rollouts, while none of the other five models did so (Figure 9). The Step 6 run used the router's default provider and recorded 19 of 24 such early completions. It passed 11 of 24 rollouts, compared with 13 of 24 in the DeepInfra run. Both counts use the same test: whether the model called mark_task_complete in its first response.

Figure 9. raman-lab rollout outcomes by when the agent declared completion. Left: the agent observed command output first. Right: it called mark_task_complete in its first response.

The comparison also shows the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

Inference for all six models cost under $5 at the router's list prices. The median raman-lab rollout used about 6,000 tokens for gpt-oss-120b and about 90,000 for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash. The companion repository holds the traces, the per-rollout results, and the scripts to add another model.

Reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. We could reuse them because Harbor and Terminal-Bench publish their code and tasks.

Task: We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. The new work was a narrower claim, skill coverage, and instructions for raman-lab.

Task data: The original spectrum served as a starting example. We built a generator for eight spectra with known parameters and reviewed them manually.

Environment: Harbor's environment support and HF Sandbox ran the tasks. We checked package requirements and diagnosed missing dependencies.

Agent harness and tools: Terminus-2 with shell access, with Inference Providers for model responses. This part needed no new work.

Rollout and trace: Harbor's rollout records and ATIF captured each run. We reviewed successes and failures and grouped them by cause.

Reference solution: We kept the convention of running solution/solve.sh and wrote a reference fit for each new task.

Evaluation harness: Harbor ran in an HF Job. We configured the run and grouped results by task.

Verifier: We reused the tests/test.sh entry point and its way of writing the score to a file. The new work was fit and ratio checks, plus tests for shortcuts and incorrect outputs.

Agent harness: The software around a model that turns its responses into actions, such as shell commands. Terminus-2 is the agent harness in this post.

Agentic evaluation: An evaluation that scores what an agent changed in an environment, not only the text it returned.

ATIF: Agent Trajectory Interchange Format, a shared format for recording an agent's messages, tool calls and observations.

Canary string: A unique marker in benchmark files that lets model trainers find and exclude them from training data.

Clustered standard error: A standard error that treats rollouts of the same task as related, which gives a wider and more honest margin than treating each rollout as independent.

Container image: A fixed package of operating system, files and software, so every rollout starts from the same environment.

Contamination: Test questions or solutions appearing in training data, so a score may reflect memory rather than skill.

Context limit: The maximum amount of text, counted in tokens, that a model can read in one request.

D, G and 2D peaks: Features in graphene's Raman spectrum. G and 2D indicate the number of layers, and D appears when the carbon lattice has defects.

Defect ratio: The intensity of the D peak divided by that of the G peak, used to indicate defects in graphene. Also called the D-to-G ratio.

Development set: Tasks used while building and debugging an evaluation, as opposed to a held-back test set used for final scores.

Environment: The software, files and resources an agent works in during a task.

Evaluation harness: The software that runs tasks, repeats rollouts, collects traces and aggregates scores. Harbor is the evaluation harness in this post.

Gated dataset: A Hugging Face dataset that can be downloaded only after the owner approves an access request.

Harbor: An open-source evaluation harness for agentic tasks.

HF Job: Compute on Hugging Face that runs a script. Here it runs Harbor.

HF Sandbox: An isolated Hugging Face environment where a single rollout runs its commands and stores its files.

Held-out test set: Test items kept private so that models cannot be trained or tuned on them.

Inference Providers: A Hugging Face service that routes model requests to third-party providers through one API, called the router.

Lorentzian: A mathematical curve commonly used to model the shape of a spectral peak.

No-op agent: An agent that does nothing. A sound evaluation gives it a score of zero.

Open-weight model: A model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run.

Oracle: An agent that runs the reference solution, used to check that every task can be solved in the supplied environment.

pass@k: The share of tasks where at least one of k rollouts succeeds.

pass^k: The share of tasks where all k rollouts succeed.

Pinning: Fixing the exact versions of software, images or model providers so a run can be repeated.

Quantization: Storing model weights at lower numerical precision to run faster and cheaper, which can change outputs slightly.

Raman shift: The difference in frequency between the laser light and the light a sample scatters, measured in cm⁻¹.

Raman spectroscopy: A technique that shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the scattered light to identify properties of the material.

Reference solution: A known correct way to complete a task, stored with the task.

Rollout: One attempt by an agent at one task. Harbor calls it a trial.

Run record: A record of what ran behind a score: the exact task, environment, model configuration and code versions.

Saturation: The point where most models reach top scores on a benchmark, so it no longer separates them.

Synthetic data: Data generated from known parameters, so the correct answer is known in advance.

Terminal-Bench: An open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a computer terminal.

Terminus-2: The terminal agent harness used in this post. It connects the model to shell commands.

Token: The unit of text a model reads and writes, roughly a short word or part of a word.

Trace: The full record of a rollout: the model's messages, its tool calls and what each command returned. Also called a trajectory.

Verifier: The code that grades a rollout by checking the saved output or the environment's final state.

Explore daily Hugging Face Hub statistics

Agentic evaluations are important for understanding how reliably AI agents perform across different tasks and scenarios. I think AI agent observability is equally valuable because tracking an agent’s behavior, decisions, and performance helps identify issues and improve results over time. This is also relevant to practical business applications such as automated customer verification, as discussed here: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/ai-kyc-automation-customer-verification

#9727. CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud

The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

#9726. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?


SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

What is SEMrush?


SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Features

  • Most accurate keyword data: Accurate keyword search volume data is crucial for SEO and PPC campaigns by allowing you to identify what keywords are most likely to bring in big sales from ad clicks. SEMrush constantly updates its databases and provides the most accurate data.
  • Largest Keyword database: SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool now features 20-billion keywords, providing marketers and SEO professionals the largest database of keywords.

  • All SEMrush users receive daily ranking data, mobile volume information, and the option to buy additional keywords by default with no additional payment or add-ons needed
  • Most accurate position tracking tool: This tool provides all subscribers with basic tracking capabilities, making it suitable for SEO professionals. Plus, the Position Tracking tool provides local-level data to everyone who uses the tool.
  • SEO Data Management: SEMrush makes managing your online data easy by allowing you to create visually appealing custom PDF reports, including Branded and White Label reports, report scheduling, and integration with GA, GMB, and GSC.
  • Toxic link monitoring and penalty recovery: With SEMrush, you can make a detailed analysis of toxic backlinks, toxic scores, toxic markers, and outreach to those sites.
  • Content Optimization and Creation Tools: SEMrush offers content optimization and creation tools that let you create SEO-friendly content. Some features include the SEO Writing Assistant, On-Page SEO Check, er/SEO Content Template, Content Audit, Post Tracking, Brand Monitoring.

Ahrefs



Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Features

  • Backlink alerts data and new keywords: Get an alert when your site is linked to or discussed in blogs, forums, comments, or when new keywords are added to a blog posting about you.
  • Intuitive interface: The intuitive design of the widget helps you see the overall health of your website and search engine ranking at a glance.
  • Site Explorer: The Site Explorer will give you an in-depth look at your site's search traffic.
  • Domain Comparison
  • Reports with charts and graphs
  • JavaScript rendering and a site audit can identify SEO issues.
  • A question explorer that provides well-crafted topic suggestions

Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

User Interface

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

  • You can see analytics from the dashboard, including search engine rankings to domain ratings, referring domains, and backlink
  • Jumping from one tool to another is easy. You can use the Keyword Explorer to find a keyword to target and then directly track your ranking with one click.
  • The website offers a tooltip helper tool that allows you to hover your mouse over something that isn't clear and get an in-depth explanation.

SEMRUSH



When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

You'll also find some other options like

  • A search bar allows you to enter a domain, keyword, or anything else you wish to explore.
  • A menu on the left side of the page provides quick links to relevant information, including marketing insights, projects, keyword analytics, and more.
  • The customer support resources located directly within the dashboard can be used to communicate with the support team or to learn about other resources such as webinars and blogs.
  • Detailed descriptions of every resource offered. This detail is beneficial for new marketers, who are just starting.

WHO WINS?

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

Rank Tracking

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

Ahrefs



The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRUSH



SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

All subscribers are given regular data updates and mobile search rankings upon subscribing

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

WHO WINS?

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword Research

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

  • It can search multiple keywords in a single search and analyze them together. At SEMrush, you also have this feature in Keyword Overview.
  • Ahrefs has a variety of keywords for different search engines, including Google, YouTube, Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, and other search engines.
  • When you click on a keyword, you can see its search volume and keyword difficulty, but also other keywords related to it, which you didn't use.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

The Keyword Magic Tool also lets you to:

  • Show performance metrics by keyword
  • Search results are based on both broad and exact keyword matches.
  • Show data like search volume, trends, keyword difficulty, and CPC.
  • Show the first 100 Google search results for any keyword.
  • Identify SERP Features and Questions related to each keyword
  • SEMrush has released a new Keyword Gap Tool that uncovers potentially useful keyword opportunities for you, including both paid and organic keywords.

WHO WINS?

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Competitor Analysis

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

AHREFS



Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

WHO WINS?

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

Pricing

Ahrefs

  • Lite Monthly: $99/month
  • Standard Monthly: $179/month
  • Annually Lite: $990/year
  • Annually Standard: $1790/year

SEMRUSH

  • Pro Plan: $119.95/month
  • Guru Plan:$229.95/month
  • Business Plan: $449.95/month

Which SEO tool should you choose for digital marketing?

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Consider choosing Ahrefs if you

  • Like friendly and clean interface
  • Searching for simple keyword suggestions

  • Want to get more keywords for different search engines like Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, Baidu, and more

 

Consider SEMrush if you:

  • Want more marketing and SEO features
  • Need competitor analysis tool
  • Need to keep your backlinks profile clean
  • Looking for more keyword suggestions for Google

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9725. Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000

Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a new state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here.

One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs (sm100), leaving out sm120 cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ.

We wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint. Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs, and let it run experiments for an afternoon.

Across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb.

The inference-optimisation skill gives an agent a fixed experimental protocol and a small, engine-agnostic benchmark script (bench.py):

bench.py measures single-user decode, aggregate decode at concurrency N, cold prefill at several lengths, and TTFT, using token counts directly from the server's usage response. All runs used a fixed panel of six prompts (code, an explanation, a story, a comparison table, a bash script, and a history summary) at temperature 1.0 (the model's default), thinking on, 512 output tokens, and 12 repetitions whenever speculative decoding was enabled.

The skill was written for a local GPU, so we adapted it to Hugging Face infrastructure:

The baseline was our existing org endpoint config: SGLang with --attention-backend fa4 and no speculative decoding.

Single-user decode speed (median of 12 requests). vLLM + DSpark reaches ~95% of the memory-bandwidth ceiling at its measured acceptance rate.

¹ SGLang's RTX PRO 6000 DSpark recipe caps --max-running-requests at 4. Raising it to 8 reached 660 tok/s, still behind vLLM. ² Includes ~160 ms of client-to-endpoint network round trip.

All of the speedup comes from switching to vLLM nightly (+15% over SGLang without speculation, 136 → 157 tok/s), enabling DSpark with 7 drafts and probabilistic draft sampling (+21% on top, 157 → 190.6 tok/s across four runs: 189.3, 190.4, 191.1, and 190.7), and adding two memory flags so vLLM's DSpark setup actually starts on 96 GB:

Both num_speculative_tokens: 7 and draft_sample_method: "probabilistic" were validated directly: shorter draft counts (such as 5) are rejected at startup because both engines enforce the checkpoint's fixed block size, and switching to greedy draft sampling dropped vLLM decode speed by 11% at temperature 1.0 (see What didn't work).

Before tuning, the agent probed the RTX PRO 6000 inside a Job (1,469 GB/s copy bandwidth, 416 TFLOPS BF16, 792 TFLOPS FP8) and read tensor sizes from the safetensors header. Because every token makes 48 layer visits, plain decode re-reads ~2.7 GB of attention and dense weights, ~2 GB of routed experts (8 of 128 per layer), and ~0.9 GB for the LM head. At 1,469 GB/s, that gives a single-user bandwidth ceiling of ~256 tok/s. Without speculation, vLLM at 157 tok/s hits 61% of that ceiling, mostly limited by kernel launch latency across 48 visits.

Speculative decoding changes the memory math on an MoE. Verifying 8 positions together activates the union of their routed experts, reading roughly 40% of each layer's experts instead of 6%. At our measured acceptance of ~2.3 tokens per step at temperature 1.0 (per-position acceptance drops from 0.6 on the first draft to 0.33 and 0.19), the bandwidth ceiling falls to ~201 tok/s. At 190.6 tok/s, vLLM + DSpark is already at ~95% of hardware bandwidth, so further flag tuning has almost nowhere left to go. Moving past 190 tok/s would take a drafter with higher acceptance at temperature 1.0 or a verification path that touches fewer experts per layer.

Most candidate flags were unsupported, noisy, or slower:

We also skipped rejection_sample_method: "fly" and "synthetic" on purpose because they alter the output distribution, and we wanted a strictly lossless speedup.

A few measurement issues caught us along the way:

Before deploying, we pinned the exact vLLM nightly digest (vllm/vllm-openai@sha256:eaa63fd6…, build 0.34.0rc1.dev1235+gf2f9edcac) and ran the acceptance gates inside a Job:

Once those passed, we deployed the endpoint with a single hf endpoints deploy command, pinning both the image digest and model revision (authenticated access, scale-to-zero after 60 idle minutes):

Running bench.py against the live endpoint gave 194.9 tok/s single-user, matching the Job runs once network latency is accounted for.

Everything from this run (PLAN.md, THEORY.md, jobs/driver.py, submit.sh, deploy.sh, and the raw ledger-*.jsonl files) is in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb. To reuse the loop on another model, put your candidate and control server commands into a configs/plan-*.json file and submit it to whichever HF Jobs GPU flavor matches your target endpoint.

There is Dflash2 for it already.Quite a bit faster.
