#9724. Valory Unveils Onchainbench to Test How Safely and Reliably AI Agents Use Crypto Wallets

The world's leading crypto & blockchain press release distribution platform.

The world's leading crypto & blockchain press release distribution platform.

The world's leading crypto & blockchain press release distribution platform.

Zurich, Switzerland, November 26th, 2026/Chainwire/--Valory, a research and deployment company at the intersection of crypto and AI and core contributor to Olas, today announced the launch of OnchainBench, an open benchmark for AI agents that use crypto wallets.

As payment providers begin trialling AI agents that can move money on behalf of businesses, OnchainBench gives users, developers and researchers a way to measure two outcomes: how successful AI agents are at completing onchain tasks and whether they can do so safely. Rolling out initially for nine EVM blockchains - Ethereum, Gnosis, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Polygon, Celo, Mode, and Robinhood, Valory aims to extend coverage to more blockchains and protocols over time.

Recently, Coinbase began rolling out controls that let users set trading limits and choose which crypto products their AI agents can trade, while Solana introduced payment channels that let agents make repeated payments within a preset spending limit and settle the total on-chain. As crypto platforms give agents more authority to trade and spend, how they respond to ambiguous user requests and misleading information can have financial consequences.

Separately, a study led by University of Oxford researchers found that deceptive content on test websites redirected agents from their assigned tasks in 25% of trials on average across six leading AI models. Together, these developments raise a question for companies giving agents control over crypto funds: how does the system respond under different attack scenarios?

Dr David Minarsch, Co-founder & CEO of Valory and Founding Member of Olas said, “Crypto scams already exploit the gap between the transaction a user intends to make and the one they end up authorising. As users delegate trading and payments to AI agents, that same gap can appear in the software acting on their behalf. An agent can handle a routine swap correctly and still be misled into moving funds without permission or with misleading information. By testing a rich set of tasks, modelled after real use cases including containing potential attack vectors, and measuring the resulting changes in wallet balances, OnchainBench gives researchers a consistent way to compare how agents perform and where their safeguards fail.”

In OnchainBench’s first evaluation, agents moved funds to an attacker in approximately 0.7% of nearly 1,800 attack tests (13 of 1,793), while task-completion scores ranged from 88.4% to 96.2%. Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex met the benchmark’s safety bar when running DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, while on their makers’ own frontier models, both missed it.

With DeepSeek, Claude Code topped the leaderboard, completing 96.2% of tasks and losing funds in one of 262 attack tests, while Codex completed 88.4% with no observed fund losses across 262 attack tests. The benchmark launches with 147 held-out tasks, including 53 safety twins designed to test agents’ responses to attacks, each task is run up to 5 times for each agent.

Following Anthropic’s IPO last week, one result stands out: in Anthropic’s own Claude Code harness, its model lost funds in more attack tests than DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, raising the question of whether provider-imposed limits on how models can be used might have unintended consequences for agent safety in crypto.

As agents gain the ability to trade and make payments autonomously, the benchmark gives developers a common way to compare how reliably they handle funds. OnchainBench runs transactions through a smart-account wallet on isolated copies of nine blockchains initially - Ethereum, Gnosis, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Polygon, Celo, Mode, and Robinhood, measuring whether agents complete tasks as instructed and how often attempts to manipulate them result in fund losses in the test environment. The benchmark covers swaps on Uniswap v3, lending on Aave v3 and token transfers, alongside tasks that test whether an agent can recover from a crash or ask a user to clarify an instruction before acting.

Valory manages OnchainBench and also develops olas-ocb-agent, one of the agents on the leaderboard. Outside agent builders can submit their own harnesses, and protocols and research teams can propose new tasks.

The benchmark is available at OnchainBench.ai, with code and result datasets on GitHub. To propose a task or submit a harness, follow the instructions on the site. Onchainbench.ai/methodology explains how tasks are scored and how attack outcomes are counted.

Valory is a research and deployment company at the intersection of crypto and AI. Specifically, the premier creator of open-source frameworks for co-owned AI. Valory’s mission is to enable communities, organizations, and countries to co-own AI systems, beginning with decentralized autonomous agents. Valory is the VC-backed team of engineers, researchers, and commercial executors that co-founded the Olas DAO, contributes to the Olas Protocol and Olas Stack, and built the first agents using Olas.

Olas is the platform that enables true co-ownership of AI. With Olas’ Pearl, the first AI Agent App Store, any consumer with a laptop can use AI agents they truly own. With Olas’ Mech Marketplace, the “AI Agent Bazaar”, businesses can put their AI agent up for hire to earn crypto and tap into other AI agents’ services. Today, Olas’ AI Agents serve diverse use cases - from prediction markets and asset management to influencer agents - autonomously creating valuable outcomes. As of September 2026, Olas has processed over 21.1M agentic transactions. The OLAS utility token provides access to the platform’s benefits and coordinates agent interactions in entire AI Agent economies. Launched in 2021 as one of the first Crypto x AI projects, today, Olas powers the largest AI agent economies with millions of transactions. Learn more at olas.network.

#9723. An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA

Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type.

We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps.

A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent:

If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up.

CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things:

The key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it.

Because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server.

Adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval: a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph.

Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning.

The fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything.

Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages.

A few small decisions mattered more than we expected:

You do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer:

Want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA, starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn.

Nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent.

Voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust.

This approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity.

If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core.

New to CUGA? Here are some places to start:

More CUGA posts on the Hugging Face blog:

Configurable Generalist Agent, leader in AppWorld Benchmark

Explore and use multiple web tools from a single dashboard

Two live CUGA agents, with and without policies

This is an interesting example of how voice agents can support Indic languages and make AI more accessible to diverse users. I think AI agent cost optimization is also worth considering when developing voice-based solutions, as managing compute resources and usage costs can help make these applications more practical to scale. #9722. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

 


Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

What is Sellfy?

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Features

Sellfy includes:

Online Store

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Product hosting

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Embed options

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Payments and security

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.


Marketing and analytics tools

The Sellfy platform includes marketing and analytics tools to help you manage your online store. You can send email product updates and collect newsletter subscribers through the platform. With Sellfy, you can also offer discount codes and product upsells, as well as create and track Facebook and Twitter ads for your store. The software's analytics dashboard will help you track your best-performing products, generated revenue, traffic channels, top locations, and overall store performance.

Integrations

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy Review: Pros and Cons

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

Pros

  • Sellfy offers a free plan for those who want to test out the features before committing to a paid plan.
  • You get paid the same day you make a sale. Sellfy doesn't delay your funds as some other payment processors do. 
  • Print-on-demand services are available directly from your store, so you can sell merchandise to fans without setting up an integration. 
  • You can conduct all store-related activities via the mobile app and all online stores have mobile responsive designs.
  • Everything you need to make your website is included, including a custom domain name hosting, security for your files, and the ability to customize your store
  • The file security features can help you protect your digital property by allowing you to put PDF stamps, set download limits, and SSL encryption.
  • Sellfy provides unlimited support.
  • Sellfy provides simple and intuitive tax and VAT configuration settings.

Cons

#9721. Where scientists draw the line on AI agents

These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings.

To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies.

Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used.

Another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized.

A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge.

For many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing new ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually.

But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs.

Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis.

But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way.

Our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows.

These examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks.

These evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like.

Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process?

An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?”

Some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves.

Participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation.

Even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher said.

Context mattered, too. Having AI critique a manuscript before submission was viewed favorably by some participants, while using it to review another researcher's unpublished work raised concerns. The distinction involves more than technical capability; peer review carries responsibilities around confidentiality, attribution, and the fair evaluation of others' research.

These disagreements suggest that responsible automation cannot be defined by a universal list of acceptable and unacceptable tasks. Scientific fields have different norms, and individual researchers may have different goals even when performing similar work.

Both are valid concerns. An agent that acts without sufficient safeguards could expose confidential data or produce harmful results, while one that’s constrained too broadly could prevent scientists from pursuing legitimate lines of inquiry.

This is why scientific communities need a meaningful role in shaping the boundaries of AI assistance. Developers need to understand not only which activities an agent can perform, but which decisions researchers want to retain and where safeguards are necessary—as well as where those safeguards might obstruct valuable work.

Our findings point toward an approach to scientific AI development that starts with the people who will use the technology.

Researchers should be able to examine an agent's contributions, determine which work to assign, and preserve opportunities to develop their own expertise. Achieving that will require technical features such as transparent records of agent actions and granular data controls, alongside evaluations informed by the standards and practices of different scientific communities.

It will also require continued collaboration. Our study is exploratory; the findings come from interviews with 17 US-based scientists, not a representative survey of scientific opinion or an empirical evaluation of specific AI agents. Participants discussed both the generative AI tools they use today and what they anticipate from more autonomous systems. Their perspectives identify important concerns and design priorities, rather than establishing a consensus about how AI should be used in science.

Still, they offer a path forward. At Ai2, we believe AI can accelerate scientific discovery while preserving the openness, reproducibility, and independent scrutiny that make research trustworthy. Through our broader efforts to develop and evaluate scientific agents, we aim to put those principles into practice. That means working with scientists to identify worthwhile uses for agents and translating their concerns into concrete evaluations, in addition to making it easier to understand both what these systems accomplish and how they accomplish it.

The promise of scientific AI isn't simply that researchers can pass off more work. It's that they can pursue questions that might otherwise be out of reach while retaining the knowledge, judgment, and agency needed to make discoveries that are their own.

Orlando, United States, November 26th, 2026/TechnologyWire/--Attorneys.org has relaunched as a complete legal resource, bringing together a national directory of trusted attorneys and law firms, plain-language legal information, and current legal news in one place. The new platform is built for how people search today, with attorney and firm profiles and legal guides structured so that both search engines and AI assistants can find, understand, and cite them.

For more than 10 years, Attorneys.org has helped people find legal representation and understand the issues in front of them. The redesign builds on that history and brings the brand in line with a major shift in how legal help is found.

Many people now skip the list of search results entirely and ask an AI assistant a full question about their situation, then act on the answer. Those answers depend on the quality of the sources behind them, and Attorneys.org has been rebuilt to be one of the sources they draw from.

Every page on the site is organized and marked up with structured data, so the details of an attorney's background or the facts in a legal guide can be read accurately by people, search engines, and AI tools. The directory lists more than 186,000 attorneys nationwide and can be searched by legal issue, attorney name, firm name, or location.

State, city, and practice area pages make it easy to see who handles a given type of case in a given place. Each profile presents an attorney's experience, practice areas, awards, and contact information in a consistent format, and law firm pages connect each firm to its attorneys.

The legal information library has been rewritten from start to finish. Each guide explains a legal issue in everyday language, answers the questions people ask most often, and cites the statutes and rules that apply. Material that no longer reflects current law has been removed, so readers and AI tools alike are working from accurate, up-to-date information.

Attorneys.org also keeps visitors informed beyond the guides. Legal News covers developments in the law that affect individuals, families, and businesses, and the Attorneys.org Podcast gives listeners a closer look at the law firms and attorneys featured in the directory.

Together, these pieces give people one dependable place to turn when a legal problem comes up. Someone can read about their issue, follow the news that affects it, and find an experienced attorney who handles that kind of case, all without leaving Attorneys.org.

Attorneys.org is a national legal resource that has connected people with trusted attorneys and reliable legal information for more than 10 years. Its directory features over 186,000 attorneys across 71 practice areas in every state, searchable by legal issue, attorney name, firm name, or location. Alongside the directory, Attorneys.org publishes plain-language legal guides, current legal news, and a podcast featuring law firms from across the country. Built for the AI search era, the platform is structured so that search engines and AI assistants can find, understand, and cite its attorney profiles and legal content, making Attorneys.org a dependable source wherever people look for legal help.

To learn more, search the directory, or read the latest legal guides and news, users can visit Attorneys.org.

#9719. I Locked Myself Out of My Own Server by Changing One Line

Every hardening guide says the same thing: move SSH off port 22 and the bots will mostly leave you alone. So one evening I opened /etc/ssh/sshd_config on a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 server, changed one line, and restarted SSH.

No errors. I opened a second terminal to try the new port.

"Refused" is a very specific word. It means my request reached the server and the server said nothing is listening there. So I checked what SSH was actually listening on:

Port 22. Still. The file said 2222, the restart had worked, and SSH did not care.

It took me an embarrassingly long time to find out why. Since Ubuntu 22.10, SSH is started by a systemd socket, ssh.socket, and the socket is what owns the port. The Port line in sshd_config is only picked up when systemd regenerates that socket, and restarting the ssh service doesn't do that. This does:

I tried again, and this time nothing happened at all. No "refused". The cursor just sat there until:

A timeout is a different animal. Refused means someone answered "no". Timed out means nobody answered, usually because something in between threw the packets away. In my case that something was UFW. Weeks earlier I had run ufw allow OpenSSH, which opens port 22. Nobody had ever told it about 2222.

And here's the part I'm least proud of. To "test cleanly", I had already closed my original session. SSH was no longer on 22, the firewall was blocking 2222, and I had no way in.

What saved me was the browser console in my VPS control panel. It's like plugging a screen and keyboard into the server: no SSH, no firewall in the way. I logged in as root with the password I had almost forgotten I had, and ran the one command I should have run first:

Back in, from my own terminal, in about thirty seconds. The whole lockout lasted maybe twenty minutes. It felt much longer.

Feeling confident again, I did the next thing on the hardening list. I created a normal user, copied root's authorized_keys into the new user's home folder with sudo cp, and switched off root login. Then:

The key was right. I checked it three times. The problem was the word sudo. The copied file still belonged to root and kept its private permissions, and SSH reads authorized_keys as the user who is logging in. My new user wasn't allowed to read its own key file. SSH doesn't explain that, it just quietly ignores the key.

Logged straight in. This time, luckily, I had kept my root session open in another tab.

I keep a second session open whenever I touch SSH or the firewall. If the change breaks something, that session is still my way in.

I open the new port in the firewall before I move SSH to it, never after.

I run sudo sshd -t after every edit. No output means the config is valid. One typo in that file can take SSH down entirely.

And I read the error message properly, because the three common ones mean very different things:

When I'm stuck on a new variation, I go through a longer checklist for each of these SSH errors instead of guessing.

Moving SSH to 2222 did cut down the noise in my auth log. It also cost me an evening and a little pride. The port change was never the real problem, though. Changing things on a live server while having only one way in was.

#9717. Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems

Part 1: Understanding swarms and training to communicate

This is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models.

That's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50.

Multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we update when we're dealing with many agents?

In this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from.

First, we'll start off with some context on swarms.

We've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI announced that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem.

But swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so.

A big swarm isn't, by itself, evidence that cooperation helped. Noam Brown estimates that less than 10% of the Navier-Stokes result came from multi-agent cooperation. In Anthropic's vulnerability-finding experiment, coordinated agents found more bugs than independent agents, but also searched more code and used more tokens. When the comparison was restricted to the same directories, the results per million tokens were about the same.

Start with the simplest case. If four agents each try a task independently, the chance that at least one gets it right is higher than with a single attempt, as long as we can tell which answer is correct. That makes a useful baseline for a multi-agent system, but it doesn't show that the agents helped each other. They may simply have had more tries.

Four attempts also cost four times as much. So the fairer comparison is at an equal budget: if each of four agents gets a quarter of the total tokens, can they still beat one agent that spends all of them? We can only find out by testing, because the answer depends on the task, the model and how the work is divided.

This series keeps asking one question: when agents communicate, does it actually help, or are we just spending more compute?

We understand that question through this simple expectation.

We'll treat agent count as a scaling dimension, alongside tokens and model size. Sometimes adding agents will help. Sometimes coordination will consume the budget we hoped to save. The point is to measure both. We won't start with 10,000 agents. We'll start with a small team on a task that we can check easily.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning has studied cooperation and competition long before language models were called swarms.

A single agent's task is a Markov decision process: observe, act, get a reward. In a team, everyone shares the reward, but each agent sees only part of the world. This is a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process: teammates, but no one sees the whole picture.

This creates three practical problems. First, teammates keep changing while each agent learns. Second, credit assignment: when the team succeeds, which actions deserve the credit? A winning team can include weak actions, and we may end up rewarding them. Third, a message changes what other agents observe, so communication is part of the policy we're training.

A common solution is centralized training with decentralized execution: training uses information from the whole team, but each agent acts only on its own observations. Our first example follows this pattern with a shared team reward.

Agents can also be organized in different ways. Two useful starting points are:

A hierarchy. A lead agent assigns work to workers and collects their results. Anthropic's Research system works this way, with a separate context for each worker. Kimi K2.5's PARL trains only the orchestrator and keeps the subagents frozen, so training a multi-agent system doesn't mean updating every component. See Anthropic's system description and Kimi's technical blog.

A distributed team. Peers send each other messages and decide when to read their inboxes. No lead agent assigns the actions. This is the setup we'll use here, following the information-aggregation task in s³: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL.

We'll reproduce the information-sharing task from Simple Scaling of Swarms because it's interpretable and straightforward to implement. Four agents share a small language model and learn to pool what each of them knows.

Each agent receives one integer from 1 to 99. It knows its own assignment and its teammates' names. It does not initially know the other agents' numbers. For example, four private assignments might be "five", "twenty-six", "five" and "seventy-eight". Duplicates stay in the list, so a correct final answer is:

The team succeeds when at least one agent submits the complete, correctly sorted list. One correct answer is enough; success does not require all four agents to answer correctly. An agent cannot reliably infer the other private assignments without information from its teammates.

This means the task does not yet test Figure 1 directly. Each agent holds information the others need, so a single agent, or a team without messaging, cannot succeed however many retries it gets. Instead, the task tests the precondition behind Figure 1: can a small shared policy learn to communicate at all, and how many tokens does that cost? A later post moves to a task that a single agent can solve alone, where the matched-budget comparison is meaningful.

The main communication tools are message(to, text), read_messages(), and check_notifications(). A notification tells an agent that unread messages exist; reading its inbox makes their contents available. Agents can send direct messages or broadcast to everyone.

We defined a four-agent system using one shared Qwen3-0.6B policy, with separate contexts and private inputs. We are not training four different models. The prompt explains the task and the tools, including the need to share assignments.

In this post, a team means one episode: four agents attempting one problem once. A successful team receives a reward reduced by the tokens it uses. A failed team receives zero:

For illustration, a correct team using half its allowance receives 0.875. There is no separate reward for sending messages. The incentive is to solve the task while using fewer generated tokens.

For every training problem, we collect eight independent team attempts. Their rewards are normalized within that group. An attempt that does better than its group average gets a positive advantage; one that does worse gets a negative advantage. Every agent in the same team receives that team's advantage, including an agent whose own final answer was wrong.

In TRL, each agent's sampled tokens form a training row. Its incoming messages and tool results provide context. The loss is averaged within each team and then across teams, so longer conversations do not give a team more weight.

Our results come from the original experiment, which used 256 team attempts per update (32 problems with eight attempts each). The walkthrough uses TRL's default of --teams-per-update 128, which works out to about 150 team attempts per update.

Over 75 steps, training success rose from 6.6% to 82.3%, comparing the first and last five updates. At checkpoint 75, the four-agent team solved 26 of 32 held-out problems (81.25%). The paper reports 93.2% four-agent success after 200 updates.

The team also used 37.4% fewer tokens per attempt, falling from about 13k to 8k. This improvement accompanied more active information sharing: broadcasts increased from 2.38 to 5.73 per team, even as total token use fell.

The team also used fewer tokens later in training. Comparing the first five updates with updates 71–75:

That is a 37.4% reduction in generated tokens per training team between those windows. At batch 75 itself, the mean was 7,624 tokens per team. These are training measurements; we did not retain held-out token-efficiency measurements for the trained checkpoint.

Notice that fewer tokens did not mean fewer messages. More agents began participating but broadcasting became more common, rather than direct messaging. Generated tokens include reasoning and tool calls as well as message bodies, so message count alone does not tell us how much text the team produced.

No agent can solve the problem alone, so the closest equivalent of "a single agent with more retries" is the untrained team with more retries. The training data already contains this comparison. Each update collects eight attempts per problem, and the task's answers are easy to check, so we can count a problem as solved when any of its eight attempts succeeded. Early in training, that count gives the untrained team's best-of-8 success rate:

With eight retries, the untrained team solves fewer than half the problems and spends about 13 times as many tokens as one attempt from the trained team. Read this as an estimate. Both rows use training problems rather than held-out ones, and updates 2–5 already sample from a slightly trained policy.

The model is small, but the rollouts are not. Each update generates millions of tokens of agent conversation at contexts of up to 40k tokens. We used one H200 for the trainer and seven H200s running vLLM rollout engines to get through those rollouts quickly, and kept each worker's eight attempts together. The walkthrough below runs the same task on two GPUs. Here are the infra details:

The figures above describe our original 75-update experiment. In this walkthrough we'll run TRL's swarm example on Hugging Face Jobs. One H200 serves the shared Qwen3-0.6B policy with vLLM and a second H200 trains it.

Sign in with a Hugging Face account that can run Jobs and create buckets. Replace YOUR_USERNAME with your Hub username.

Use a fresh bucket for each run so earlier measurements stay available.

Save the script below as train-swarm.sh in your current directory.

The command below sends its contents to the job. Inside the job, vLLM serves the shared policy on GPU 0. GPU 1 runs TRL's async_grpo_s3_aggregation.py for 50 updates with Trackio. TRL's evaluate.py scores the base model and checkpoint 50 on the same 192 held-out problems. That is a larger set than the 32-problem checks in our results, which gives tighter error bars. The job saves both scores, the checkpoint, Trackio data and the exact Git commit to your bucket.

One TRL rollout contains a whole team conversation. The trainer compares eight attempts at the same problem and gives all four agents in an attempt the same advantage. Each update uses about 150 team attempts. TRL packs micro-batches by token count rather than by team, so the --teams-per-update 128 setting is approximate. The --report-to trackio flag records training metrics at every update.

This shorter run is cheaper than our original experiment, and it stops earlier on the learning curve. TRL's run of this example took about 4.8 hours on two H100s and reached 60.9% held-out success at checkpoint 50.

To run closer to our original experiment, change the training flags to --updates 75 --teams-per-update 256 --concurrent-teams 256, replace checkpoint-50 with checkpoint-75 in the script, and raise the job's --timeout to 24h. That is three times as many rollouts. The two codebases still differ in details such as the system prompt, so expect similar results rather than an exact replication.

Once the job completes, sync the bucket to a local folder. It holds the two evaluation files, the Trackio data, the TRL revision and the checkpoint-50 weights, which are the largest download. In the dashboard, compare team/success, team/messages and team/tokens over training. The job logs also give the held-out success rate for the base model and checkpoint 50. Each line of base.jsonl or trained.jsonl records one of those evaluation attempts.

This first example gives us a small environment, a shared reward and a policy that improves at pooling private information. It also shows why success, token use and communication structure need to be read together. At 75 updates, the team is solving most checked problems, but it has not converged to the cleanest communication pattern.

In the coming examples, we'll take a step back from training and look at how we evaluate and analyze swarms.

For now, we have something concrete to build on: four small agents, one trainable policy, a checkable task, and a reproducible way to examine what the team learned.

#9715. The Illusion of the “Kill Switch”: Why Removing a User From SSO Doesn’t Always Revoke Access

I am a Product Manager trying to bridge the gap between complex customer requirements and high-impact technical execution.

I am a Product Manager trying to bridge the gap between complex customer requirements and high-impact technical execution.

I am a Product Manager trying to bridge the gap between complex customer requirements and high-impact technical execution.

Every week, a company terminates an engineer or a sales rep with access to sensitive production data. As part of the offboarding checklist, the IT administrator logs into Okta or Microsoft Entra ID, finds the employee's profile, and clicks Deactivate.

The IT admin closes their laptop, confident that the employee is locked out of the company’s entire SaaS stack.

Twenty minutes later, that terminated employee opens their personal laptop, refreshes an open browser tab for your B2B SaaS application, and exports the entire customer database. Or worse, a Python script on their local machine continues pulling records via a Personal Access Token (PAT) for the next six months.

Why did this happen? Because SAML and OIDC only govern the front door. Once a user is inside your application, your Identity Provider (IdP) is completely blind to what happens next.

If you are building a B2B SaaS product, relying on SSO login checks alone means your enterprise customers have a massive, silent offboarding vulnerability. Here is a technical breakdown of the four architectural gaps that keep terminated users active and how to engineer the fixes.

How the problem gets built: When a user logs in via SAML 2.0 or OIDC, the IdP hands your Assertion Consumer Service (ACS) endpoint a signed payload saying: "As of 9:00:00 AM, Alice is an active employee."

Why it fails during offboarding: If Alice is terminated at 9:15 AM and removed from Okta, Okta does not notify your application in a standard SAML setup. Your API gateway continues to validate Alice's stateless JWT strictly by checking its cryptographic signature and its exp timestamp. Because the signature is still valid, Alice has uninterrupted access for the remaining 23 hours and 45 minutes.

The Architectural Fix: Short-Lived Access Tokens + Stateful Refresh Revocation \ Never issue long-lived stateless JWTs for enterprise tenants. Split your session architecture into two tiers:

When the 15-minute JWT expires, the browser must hit your /auth/refresh endpoint. This forces a stateful lookup where your backend can verify that tenant_memberships.status == 'ACTIVE' before minting a new 15-minute JWT.

How the problem gets built: Many engineering teams build SAML/OIDC login + Just-In-Time (JIT) user creation and consider "Enterprise SSO" complete. They skip building a SCIM 2.0 (System for Cross-domain Identity Management) server because customers only ask about SAML during the initial trial.

Why it fails during offboarding: JIT provisioning is a one-way street. It creates users when they log in, but it can never tell you when a user leaves. Without SCIM, your application only discovers a user was deactivated in Okta when their session finally expires and they try to log in again—which could be days or weeks later if you use rolling refresh tokens.

The Architectural Fix: Wiring SCIM PATCHto a Kill-Switch WorkerWhen you implement a SCIM 2.0/Users/{id} endpoint, deactivating a user in Okta or Entra ID immediately triggers an outbound HTTP request to your backend:

Do not treat this PATCH request as a simple database update (UPDATE users SET active = false). It must execute an Atomic Revocation Cascade:

By pushing revoked_user:{tenant_id}:{user_id} into Redis with a 15-minute TTL (matching your JWT lifetime), your API gateway can check a sub-millisecond Redis key on every request and kill the user's in-flight JWT within milliseconds of the IT admin clicking "Deactivate" in Okta.

How the problem gets built: Even when teams remember to invalidate web browser sessions, they forget about secondary authentication channels created by the user while they were employed:

Why it fails during offboarding: In many schemas, API keys are validated by a simple lookup on the api_keys table (SELECT tenant_id, scopes FROM api_keys WHERE key_hash = :hash). Notice what is missing in that query: it never joins against the users or tenant_memberships table to verify if the creator of the key is still employed.

You must enforce a strict separation in your data model between Human-Bound Credentials and Machine Service Accounts:

What Happens When User is Removed from SSO?

Immediately Revoked. Any API call using this token must fail with 401 Unauthorized the moment the user's tenant_membership is deactivated.

Immediately Revoked. Refresh tokens issued to third-party apps on behalf of this user are purged.

Remains Active (With Audit Alert). Never let critical production CI/CD pipelines run on a human engineer's PAT. Provide dedicated Service Accounts owned by the Tenant, and fire a warning notification to workspace admins if the user who originally created the Service Account is deprovisioned so they can rotate the secret if needed.

How the problem gets built: Before Acme Corp upgraded to your Enterprise tier and configured SAML SSO, five of their engineers signed up for your product using a standard email + password or "Sign in with Google." Later, Acme's IT admin configures Okta SAML in your portal.

Why it fails during offboarding: When one of those original five engineers is fired and removed from Okta, they can no longer log in via the "Sign in with SSO" button. So they go back to your login page, click "Forgot Password" (or use their old cached password / linked Google account), and log right back into the workspace—completely bypassing the Okta SAML wall.

When a tenant sets enforce_sso = TRUE on their workspace:

If you want to test whether your application actually revokes access when a user is removed from SSO, run this 5-minute test in your staging environment today:

#9714. How much do Forward-Deployed Engineers actually get paid? The live numbers.

A Forward-Deployed Engineer (FDE) is the breakout job of the AI era, but salary figures float around as folklore. So I pulled the open postings, normalized the structured salary data, and recomputed every number on every build. Here is what the live data actually shows (snapshot: 2026-11-27).

Right now there are 1,124 open FDE roles across 250 companies. Of those, 237 post a structured USD annual salary — enough to reason about real pay, not vibes.

So the honest median band for a salary-disclosing FDE role is roughly $185k at the floor and $250k at the ceiling — with a real tail of six-figure-above-band comp at the very top.

The companies posting the most salary-disclosing FDE roles: OpenAI (59), then Datadog (13), Cursor (9), Rogo (9), Temporal (7), Baseten (6). The volume is concentrated — a handful of AI-native companies drive most of the high-band supply.

If you're an FDE negotiating, the market has a hard floor around $185k and a demonstrable ceiling past $400k. If you're hiring, the six-figure-above-band tail is real but thin — 6 of 237 roles — so top-of-band offers are a genuinely scarce currency.

Every figure above is recomputed from the live job set. Related live breakdowns:

About the data. fdenotes pulls open FDE postings from major job boards and ATS providers (Greenhouse, Ashby), dedupes them, and recomputes all numbers on every build. Each data page carries its snapshot date and a copy-ready citation (APA / BibTeX) so the figures are easy to reference.

#9713. Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference

We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents.

Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference. We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion.

Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications.

Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation.

This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process.

We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training:

Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples: rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values.

Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples: rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships.

OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples: synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading.

Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language.

Figure 2. Parse recovers 18, 27, 39, and 54 from the chart geometry

We trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading a page and representing its contents.

We then continued with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Rewards check the quality of sampled extractions. For example, a chart extraction can earn a better reward for recovering the correct series and values, producing a usable structure, and finishing without repeatedly generating the same content.

A difficult page can have several valid representations. These checks give the model flexibility to find a correct answer without prescribing one exact token sequence, while discouraging looping and unfinished output.

Figure 3. A controlled comparison of SFT and GRPO with matched evaluation settings. These are development checkpoints, separate from the final released model. Loop counts use a repetition check. Methods.

The matched comparison shows the benefit: loop-flagged outputs fall from 126 to 29 pages—about 77% fewer—and outputs reaching the 9,000-token limit fall from 185 to 35. Overall score improves from 66.24 to 71.38, including +5.18 points in tables and +4.15 in charts.

A parser must generate substantial text and structure for every page. Alongside the training work, we optimized how Parse 3.5 processes images and decodes those outputs.

NaViT preprocessing adapts the input shape to the page. A visual adapter compresses the image sequence, and the text decoder consumes it as a prefix, replacing encoder–decoder cross-attention. Grouped-query attention with eight key/value heads (GQA-8) reduces the decoder’s attention-cache memory.

The built-in multi-token prediction (MTP) head supplies one-token lookahead. Our DFlash2 speculator goes further: a small draft model proposes up to 32 tokens ahead, and Parse verifies the proposals together. In the measured 32-token configuration, it averages about 14 accepted draft tokens, or roughly 15 output tokens of progress per verification step including the target token.

Figure 4. Native single-pass throughput on one H200, BF16, using the same 2,078 pages. Parse 2.0 uses one trial per point; Parse 3.5 shows three-trial medians. Arrows show the gain from Parse 3.5 base to DFlash2. Measurement details.

In the native single-pass benchmark on one H200 in BF16, DFlash2 increased throughput 7.62× at concurrency 1 and 1.52× at concurrency 512, compared with Parse 3.5 with speculative decoding disabled. At 512, Parse 3.5 reaches 13.48 pages/s without speculation and 20.44 pages/s with DFlash2, versus 2.98 for Parse 2.0. Those are 4.53× and 6.86× the Parse 2.0 throughput, respectively.

Fast parsing gives us room to revisit difficult regions. Start with a full-page prediction, then add focused reprocessing where the document needs it:

Single pass - Parse the full page once for text, layout, tables, and charts.

Double pass - use for dense tables and small chart details. Crop the table and chart regions found by the parser, re-parse them at higher detail, and merge the refinements into the page output.

Triple pass - Instead of only using the models full page parsing bounding boxes, use a second pass of the model in detection mode in order to get verification that all boxes have been accurately found and text has not been missed and re-extract any found charts or tables in a third pass

Figure 5. Additional stages focus computation on difficult regions. Multiple crops can require multiple requests.

In the published reference evaluation, double and triple pass add 2.18 and 2.46 ParseBench points over single pass. The additional work lets applications trade some throughput for better extraction in difficult regions. Reference results and serving measurements.

We are sharing a Parse fine-tuning recipe that takes developers through paired data generation, NeMo Automodel SFT, and NeMo RL GRPO, using vLLM to generate candidate answers.

The worked example uses a synthetic dental form with an odontogram: a chart showing teeth, planned procedures, and affected tooth surfaces. Before adaptation, Parse reads the printed tooth numbers but misses the intended procedure table. SFT teaches it to associate each marked tooth with a procedure and its placement on the tooth.

Figure 6. A recorded recipe example: after SFT, all six chart rows match the target. Full image and native training label.

RLVR then reinforces accuracy and consistent completion. In the dental reference run, the estimated first-attempt success rate (sampled pass@1) rose from 0.00% for the base model to 95.85% after SFT and 96.58% after RLVR.

Figure 7. Matched evaluation on 256 held-out forms from the same synthetic generator, with eight samples per page. Success requires natural completion, exact chart content, and error-free normalized page text. Evaluation protocol.

To adapt the recipe, supply your own image/label pairs and a verifier: checks that determine whether an extraction is correct. The included document reward components cover text fidelity, bounding boxes, tables, chart facts, and completion. Combine the components relevant to your task, add schema checks, and use completion and repetition checks to discourage looping or unfinished output.

We are excited that the community has extended and improved Parse for Thai, Persian/Farsi, and Arabic already and we hope that these additional datasets and fine-tuning recipes will help encourage these efforts and future models.

We thank Denis Ovchinnikov for his work on vLLM integration and independent performance validation, Oliver Holworthy for improving the fine-tuning recipe's runtime setup and reproducibility, and Bo Liu for technical review.

#9712. The Roster Problem: Every Failure Family Needs an Owner

Most subscription businesses do not have a recovery problem. They have a roster problem. Failed payments arrive in families — expired cards, soft declines, insufficient funds, issuer blocks, stale credentials after a processor change — and each family responds to a different remedy. Yet in most companies every family lands in the same undifferentiated queue, worked by whoever happens to notice it, with the same retry clock and the same email. The queue is busy. Nobody owns a family. That is why the numbers never move.

Management, in this corner of operations, is mostly assignment. An expired card is a calendar problem: it can be seen coming weeks ahead, and the fix is a prompt sent while the old card still works. A soft decline is a timing and presentation problem: the retry needs to land when the issuer is most likely to say yes, with the descriptor the customer expects. Insufficient funds is a household-cash-flow problem: the retry belongs near payday, not near the anniversary of the failure. An issuer block is a conversation problem: no retry schedule fixes it, only the customer can. Four families, four different crafts. One queue with one treatment serves none of them well.

The roster test is simple. Pick last month's failures and ask, for each family, three questions. Who noticed it first? What did they do that was specific to that family? How do we know whether it worked? In most businesses the honest answers are: the system noticed, the system did the same thing it does for everything, and nobody knows. The failure families that recover are the ones where a human can answer all three without checking a dashboard.

Tooling enters here, and it enters as an assignment aid before it enters as automation. The useful question about any platform is whether it sorts failures into families and reports recovery per family, so an owner can be named and a remedy can be judged. A single blended recovery rate hides the roster completely: a business can be excellent at expired cards and hopeless at issuer blocks, and the blend will read as average while money leaks through the one family nobody owns. Dunning management software judged as a roster system — whether it sorts failures into owned families and reports recovery per family instead of one blended rate is the standard worth holding every candidate to, because the sorting is what makes ownership possible.

Ownership also changes what improvement looks like. Without families, improvement means more: more retries, more emails, more pressure on everyone. With families, improvement means specific: the expired-card prompt moves a week earlier, the insufficient-funds retry shifts two days, the issuer-block message gets rewritten in plain language. Each change is small, testable, and attributable. A quarter of small attributable wins compounds into a failure rate that actually falls, which no amount of undifferentiated effort has ever produced.

There is a staffing honesty in this too. Naming an owner per family does not require a team. In a small business one person may own all four families — but they own them as four distinct jobs with four distinct scoreboards, done at four distinct moments in the week, not as one anxious glance at a queue. The roster is a way of thinking before it is a headcount.

Start with the sort. Print last month's failures grouped by family, write a name beside each group — even if every name is the same name — and write the one remedy that family will get this month that it did not get last month. That single page is more management than most recovery operations ever receive, and it is the page the software should be generating for you automatically.

That is the ordering behind Swipe Again's family-first approach to failed payments, where each decline family carries its own remedy and its own scoreboard — sort first, assign second, automate third, and never let a blended rate tell you the roster is fine when one family is quietly drowning.

#9711. 25 Midwestern Thanksgiving Recipes That Bring The Nostalgia (& The Flavor)

Even nicer than Midwest nice (and that's saying something!).

My holidays were split between regions growing up. We spent Thanksgiving at my dad’s side, and Christmas with my mom’s. With my mom’s Alabama and Texas roots and my dad's Missouri and Kansas roots, that meant that Christmas dinner was a Southern affair and Thanksgiving was a Midwestern feast. Both holiday spreads had a fair amount of overlap of dishes (casseroles galore), but I have to say: A classic Midwest Thanksgiving has a special place in my heart.

What makes a Midwest Thanksgiving, you may ask? All of the classics are present, plus a few surprising favorites that, in my house, no holiday is complete without. We think beyond the turkey, sometimes skip mashed potatoes for a cheesy casserole, and have to be careful not to fill up on all the rolls (butter and honey better be on the table). Ready to celebrate Midwest-style? Here are some recipes that your holiday won’t be complete without:

Made with canned pineapple, pistachio pudding, and Cool Whip, this retro crowd-pleasing dessert “salad” will take you straight back to the ’70s with just one bite. It’s the perfect recipe to throw together if you don’t have a ton of time, but you need to take something to that potluck or family gathering.

Thanksgiving is equally about food and football, so this tailgate-inspired stuffing is a no-brainer. Filled with beer cheese sauce and topped with crispy bacon, this twist on the classic holiday side is so irresistible, it’ll be gone long before halftime of that first Thanksgiving Day game.

It takes less than than 5 minutes to pour some pepper jelly over cream cheese and place some crackers around. These bites are slightly more elevated without many more steps. It’s for those that want to feel like they are putting some effort into their appetizer without it being difficult or time-consuming.

Don't be fooled by the name—the only thing deathly about this casserole is how absolutely delicious it is. This cheesy, creamy casserole is a staple at every holiday in my Kansas home, and Thanksgiving is no exception. Yes, we often have mashed potatoes too.

For this recipe, we ditched canned cream of mushroom soup and went for fresh instead. It's not how my mom makes it, but trust me—by sautéing mushrooms with sliced onion in butter, you're building a base with some serious depth of flavor. Cook the mushrooms enough that they get a little caramelized, and you'll really be good to go.

No matter the holiday, one thing is for sure: Deviled eggs will be making an appearance. Variations are always welcome (looking at you, harissa deviled eggs), but if grandpa is going to have a happy Thanksgiving, then this classic recipe better be present.

Strawberry pretzel tart, AKA strawberry pretzel salad, might sound a little strange, but trust us—it strikes the perfect balance of whimsical and classic, sweet and salty. The pretzel crust proves to be an ideal complement to the rich cream cheese layer and the sweet strawberries with their Jell-O glaze.

Turkey usually rules the roost at Thanksgiving, but it's not the only centerpiece present at many Midwestern holiday tables. Depending on how many family members are coming, my family has been known to prepare a turkey and a ham—it's the best of both worlds!

We’re certainly not opposed to roasted Brussels sprouts, but we also love giving them the traditional Thanksgiving treatment—plenty of butter, cream, and cheese. This method upgrades even the most humble vegetables while still allowing them to be the star of the show.

This sweet party dip is the perfect way to add that little extra something to your fruit spread, but your dipping options don't stop there! With just 5 minutes of prep, this is the easiest dessert that any party will be thankful for. Plus, you can easily make it ahead and travel with it, making it an ideal potluck recipe.

These Thanksgiving potato skins are piled high with leftovers, but they’re so good, they just might deserve a place in your holiday spread. The hollowed-out potatoes are an excellent vessel for extra-creamy mashed potatoes, stuffing, turkey, and dollops of cranberry sauce.

Essentially, this is chicken Alfredo, but with a few extra decadent add-ins, like cream cheese, garlic, and punchy spices like nutmeg and black pepper. When you’re craving the classic but have to serve a crowd, this is the recipe you should make.

A cheese ball is peak party appetizer nostalgia, and these cheese ball bites are here to put a new, shareable twist on the classic. They’re so simple to make, only require a handful of ingredients, and are super versatile based on what you have on hand.

I'll clarify that when I say stuffing, I'm actually referring to dressing. Traditional stuffing should be stuffed inside the turkey and cooked in there, but in my family, we've always called it stuffing. By cooking your stuffing in a baking dish, you get crunchy, buttery pieces of bread on top and soft, bread pudding-esque pieces underneath.

What’s the best kind of potato? A loaded baked potato, of course. With this in mind, we combined the two superstar spuds into one glorious dish. In it, light, airy mashed potatoes are topped with all of the classic baked potato fillings—cheddar cheese, chives, bacon, and sour cream—for a dish that truly embodies the best of both worlds.

Most sweet potato casseroles have only marshmallows or pecans. Don't even think about making this mistake. Topping with a pecan streusel and then marshmallows helps this Thanksgiving casserole stand out above all the rest.

If you’re not into creamy, melty macaroni and cheese with a wildly satisfying cheese-pull, then you might want to find another mac recipe. Sorry, but this slow-cooker macaroni and cheese is just too darn dreamy.

Step aside, all other casseroles—corn is not to be overlooked on the holiday table. If you prefer, drained and rinsed canned corn can be used instead of frozen, and you could substitute more milk in for the heavy cream. The finished casserole won't be quite as decadent, but it will still be delicious.

Deviled eggs are great, but when you have them for every holiday, it just makes sense to change them up sometimes. These are our new obsession

If green beans dressed up as cheesy garlic bread, then they would become these Parmesan roasted green beans. Tossed in garlic and black pepper and showered with cheese, this simply irresistible side dish will steal the spotlight at every holiday table.

This sweet party dip is the perfect way to add that little extra something to your fruit spread, but your dipping options don't stop there! With just 5 minutes of prep, this is the easiest dessert that any party will be thankful for.
